The evidence on whether drinking coffee can prevent type 2 diabetes is mixed and context-dependent. Long-term studies cited by Harvard's Nutrition Source show that habitual coffee drinkers have a lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared with non-drinkers, with one meta-analysis of 45,335 people finding up to a 33% decreased risk for those drinking 6 cups per day [d2]. A 2014 Harvard study tracked nearly 124,000 people and found that those who increased coffee intake by more than a cup a day had an 11% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes [d5], and Harvard's disease prevention resource describes "convincing evidence that coffee may help protect against diabetes" [d4]. Replacing a daily sugary drink with unsweetened coffee has also been associated with a 14–25% lower risk of developing the disease [d6], and Diabetes UK notes that unsweetened tea and coffee are associated with reduced risk [d7]. However, d1 cautions that "no food or supplement offers total protection against type 2 diabetes" and that "taking up drinking coffee in order to stave off diabetes won't guarantee you a good result," while d5 explicitly warns that people who already have type 2 diabetes should avoid caffeinated coffee, as caffeine raises both blood sugar and insulin levels in those with the disease [d1][d5]. The protective association appears strongest for unsweetened, plain coffee consumed habitually over the long term, and is attributed to polyphenols, magnesium, and antioxidants rather than caffeine itself [d2][d3].
